Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The set of vectors [MATH: \{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_n \}] in an abstract vector space [MATH: V] is linearly dependent if there exist real scalars [MATH: x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n] not all zero such that

Content:
[MATH: x_1\mathbf{v}_1+x_2\mathbf{v}_2+\ldots+x_n\mathbf{v}_n=\mathbf{0}.]

Content:
Otherwise, if [MATH: x_1 = x_2 = \cdots = x_n = 0] is the only solution, the set is linearly independent.

Content:
Let's consider some examples.

Content:
- First, let's consider the vector space [MATH: \mathbb{R}[t]] of all polynomials in variable [MATH: t,] along with the set
[MATH: S = \big\{ \underbrace{1}_{\color{blue}p_1(t)}, \: \underbrace{t}_{\color{blue}p_2(t)}, \: \underbrace{t^2}_{\color{blue}p_3(t)} \big\}.]
To determine whether [MATH: S] is linearly dependent in [MATH: \mathbb{R}[t],] we must solve the equation
[MATH: x_{1}p_{1}(t) + x_{2}p_{2}(t) + x_{3}p_{3}(t)|= 0.]
Substituting the given expressions for [MATH: p_1(t),p_2(t)] and [MATH: p_3(t)] into the above equation, we obtain
[MATH: x_{1} ⋅ 1 + x_{2} ⋅ t + x_{3} ⋅ t^{2}|= 0; x_{1} + x_{2}t + x_{3}t^{2}|= 0.]
The final equation is true for every [MATH: t] if and only if
[MATH: {x_{1} = 0; x_{2} = 0; x_{3} = 0.]
Since [MATH: x_1 = x_2 = x_3 = 0] is the only solution, [MATH: S] is linearly independent in [MATH: \mathbb R[t].]

Content:
- Let's consider the vector space [MATH: \mathbb R[t]] once more, along with the set
[MATH: T = \big\{ \underbrace{t^2+1}_{\color{red}q_1(t)}, \: \underbrace{-2t^2-2}_{\color{red}q_2(t)} \big\}.]
To determine whether [MATH: T] is linearly dependent in [MATH: \mathbb{R}[t],] we must solve the equation
[MATH: x_{1}q_{1}(t) + x_{2}q_{2}(t)|= 0; x_{1}(t^{2} + 1) + x_{2}(− 2t^{2} − 2)|= 0; (x_{1} − 2x_{2}) + (x_{1} − 2x_{2})t^{2}|= 0.]
The final equation is true for every [MATH: t] if and only if
[MATH: {x_{1} − 2x_{2} = 0; x_{1} − 2x_{2} = 0.]
This system has the nonzero solution [MATH: (x_1,x_2)=(2,1).] As a result, we get
[MATH: 2 \cdot {\color{red}q_1(t)} + 1 \cdot {\color{red}q_2(t)} = 0.]
Therefore, the set [MATH: \big\{ q_1(t), q_2(t) \big\}] is linearly dependent in [MATH: \mathbb R[t].]

Content:
Note the following important property of linearly dependent sets.

Content:
> A set of vectors is linearly dependent if and only if it contains a vector that is a linear combination of other vectors from that set.

Content:
To see why this is true, let [MATH: \{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2,\cdots, \mathbf{v}_n\}] be a linearly dependent set of [MATH: n] vectors. This means that the equation

Content:
[MATH: x_1\mathbf{v}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{v}_2 + \cdots + x_n\mathbf{v}_n = \mathbf{0}]
has a non-trivial solution, i.e. a solution in which at least one of the coefficients [MATH: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n] is not zero. Without loss of generality, we may assume that [MATH: x_1 \ne 0,] and we can rewrite the above equation as
[MATH: \mathbf{v}_1 = -\dfrac{x_2}{x_1} \mathbf{v}_2 - \dfrac{x_3}{x_1}\mathbf{v}_3 - \cdots - \dfrac{x_n}{x_1}\mathbf{v}_n.]

Content:
The above argument shows that the vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] can be written as a linear combination of the other vectors from the set.
